title: What Is a Virus?
description: Living or not? Either way, ubiquitous

concepts.title: The Smallest Replicators
concepts.contentHtml:
A virus is a genome (DNA or RNA) wrapped in protein, sometimes with a lipid envelope. By itself it has no metabolism — viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that hijack host cells to replicate.

Sizes from ~20 nm (parvoviruses) to over 1 µm (giant viruses such as pithovirus). Genomes from a few kb (HIV ~10 kb) to over 1 Mb (giant viruses). The smallest viruses encode just a few proteins; large ones encode hundreds.

Whether viruses are 'alive' is a philosophical question. They evolve, they replicate, they affect every other living thing. They're life-adjacent.

concepts.title: Genome Diversity
concepts.contentHtml:
Viruses come with every kind of genome: dsDNA (herpesviruses, adenoviruses), ssDNA (parvoviruses), dsRNA (rotaviruses), (+)ssRNA (poliovirus, SARS-CoV-2 — directly translatable), (-)ssRNA (flu, rabies — needs transcription first), retroviruses ((+)ssRNA reverse-transcribed to DNA, then integrated — HIV).

The Baltimore classification organizes viruses by genome type. Each type has its own replication strategy and vulnerabilities to drugs.

concepts.title: Why Viruses Outnumber Everything
concepts.contentHtml:
Estimates of total viral particles on Earth: ~10³¹ — more than every star in the observable universe.

Most are bacteriophages — viruses that infect bacteria. Each second, ~10²³ phage infections happen in the oceans. Phages drive bacterial evolution and turnover the marine carbon cycle.

Viruses are the most numerous biological entities on Earth, by far. We've sequenced a few thousand species; metagenomics suggests millions more await characterization.

concepts.title: Attachment & Entry
concepts.contentHtml:
Viruses bind specific cell-surface receptors. SARS-CoV-2's spike protein binds ACE2; HIV's gp120 binds CD4 + a co-receptor; influenza HA binds sialic acid.

Receptor specificity determines tropism — which cells (and which species) the virus can infect. Mutations in spike/HA can shift host range, sometimes triggering pandemics.

Entry is by direct membrane fusion or endocytosis. Some viruses need acid pH endosomes to trigger fusion (flu); others fuse at the plasma membrane (HIV).

concepts.title: Replication Strategies
concepts.contentHtml:
Once inside, viruses commandeer cellular machinery to replicate. DNA viruses typically use the host's polymerases. RNA viruses bring their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp).

Retroviruses are unique: their reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy of the RNA genome, which is then integrated into the host chromosome (provirus). HIV's RT is a major drug target.

Replication can be fast — herpesviruses produce ~10⁵ progeny per cell. RNA viruses also have very high mutation rates (~10⁻⁴ per base per replication for HIV vs ~10⁻⁹ for human cells).

concepts.title: Assembly & Release
concepts.contentHtml:
New viral genomes are packaged into newly synthesized capsid proteins. Many viruses use elegant self-assembly — proteins spontaneously form icosahedral or helical capsids around their genomes.

Enveloped viruses bud through host membranes, picking up a lipid coat with embedded viral proteins. Naked viruses are released by cell lysis.

Some viruses establish latency: integrate or persist inactively, reactivating later. Herpes simplex, varicella-zoster (chickenpox/shingles), HIV — all do this.

concepts.title: Antiviral Drug Targets
concepts.contentHtml:
Viruses have fewer drug targets than bacteria — they hijack host machinery, so anti-host drugs would harm us too. Effective antivirals target uniquely viral functions.

HIV combination therapy attacks reverse transcriptase, protease, integrase, and entry coreceptors. Hepatitis C is curable in 8-12 weeks with direct-acting antivirals targeting the virus's protease and polymerase.

Influenza neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir/Tamiflu) block viral release. Acyclovir is activated by herpes-encoded thymidine kinase and then blocks the viral DNA polymerase.

concepts.title: Vaccines
concepts.contentHtml:
Vaccines train immunity without causing disease. Several strategies:

• Inactivated (whole virus, killed): rabies, polio (Salk).
• Live attenuated (weakened): MMR, Sabin polio, yellow fever.
• Subunit / recombinant protein: HBV, HPV, hepatitis B surface antigen.
• mRNA: encoded antigen produced by your own cells (COVID Pfizer/Moderna).
• Viral vector: harmless virus delivers antigen gene (J&J COVID, AstraZeneca, ebola).

Smallpox eradicated (1980); polio nearly so. Vaccines have prevented an estimated ~150 million child deaths in the past 50 years.

concepts.title: Why Some Diseases Lack Vaccines
concepts.contentHtml:
Vaccines are hard for viruses with high mutation rates (HIV, influenza), highly variable surface antigens (HCV pre-DAA era), latency in host genomes, or pathogenesis that requires the very immune response itself.

HIV evades vaccines partly through extreme variability of envelope glycoproteins. Universal flu vaccines targeting conserved regions are an active goal. Malaria (parasite, not virus) is similarly vexing.

Each new pathogen tests our ability to design protection.

concepts.title: Zoonotic Spillover
concepts.contentHtml:
Most emerging human diseases come from animals. SARS, MERS, SARS-CoV-2 from bats (with possible intermediate hosts). Ebola from bats. HIV from chimps. Flu from birds and pigs.

Spillover requires a virus to encounter humans (often via wildlife trade, deforestation, agricultural intensification) and to be capable of human-to-human transmission. Most cross-species jumps fizzle; a few become epidemics.

concepts.title: Pandemic Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
The basic reproduction number R₀ is the average number of new cases caused by one infected person in a fully susceptible population. R₀ > 1 → exponential growth.

Measles R₀ ≈ 18 (very contagious). SARS-CoV-2 ancestral ≈ 2-3; later variants ~10. Common cold ~2-3.

Effective reproduction number R_eff drops with vaccination, prior infection, behavior changes. Herd immunity threshold ≈ 1 - 1/R₀ — for measles, you need 95% immune to halt spread.

concepts.title: Surveillance & Preparedness
concepts.contentHtml:
Pandemic preparedness combines viral genomic surveillance (who's circulating, who's mutating), animal monitoring (where might a spillover come from), and rapid vaccine/therapeutic platforms.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were designed within days of SARS-CoV-2 sequence release. Bioscience can now respond in months — but global manufacturing and distribution remain slow.

Bird flu (H5N1), new coronaviruses, and Nipah virus are among the candidates for the next major outbreak. Whether we've learned from COVID will be tested.

concepts.title: Phage Therapy
concepts.contentHtml:
Bacteriophages infect specific bacteria. Each phage has narrow host range — a feature, not a bug, for fighting specific infections without disturbing the rest of the microbiome.

Largely abandoned in the West after antibiotics arrived (1940s), phage therapy persisted in Eastern Europe (especially Georgia and Russia). With antibiotic resistance rising, it's making a comeback.

Compassionate-use phage therapy has saved patients with multidrug-resistant infections. Standardization and clinical trials are catching up.

concepts.title: Viral Vectors in Gene Therapy
concepts.contentHtml:
Modified viruses deliver therapeutic genes to patients. AAV (adeno-associated virus) is the workhorse for in vivo gene therapy: small, non-pathogenic, tissue-targetable.

Approved AAV gene therapies include treatments for spinal muscular atrophy (Zolgensma), inherited retinal disease (Luxturna), and hemophilia. Lentiviral vectors are used ex vivo for CAR-T cancer therapies and gene therapy for sickle cell disease.

Repurposing nature's intracellular delivery machines — viruses — has been one of biotech's quiet triumphs.

concepts.title: CRISPR — From Phage Defense to Tool
concepts.contentHtml:
CRISPR/Cas systems evolved as bacterial defense against phages — RNA-guided cutting of viral DNA. Repurposed in 2012 (Doudna, Charpentier; Nobel 2020) as a programmable gene-editing tool.

Cas9 + guide RNA → cut DNA at any specified sequence. Subsequent variants edit single bases without cutting (base editors), do search-and-replace (prime editing), or activate/repress genes (CRISPRa/i).

Casgevy (2023) — first CRISPR-edited gene therapy approved. Bacteria's defense system has reshaped human medicine.
